Château Climens 2010 is the sweet spot bottle with the Lemon Tart: bin 192821, $200.

Barsac is the village next to Sauternes in Bordeaux, on lower, limestone ground, and its sweet wines are known for a lifted freshness. Château Climens, klee-MAHNS, is a first growth of Barsac in the 1855 classification of sweet wines, farmed biodynamically. Unusually, it makes its wine from Sémillon alone. The grapes are picked by hand in several passes once noble rot has shrivelled and concentrated them, and the wine is aged in oak.

At sixteen years it is deep gold. It tastes of candied lemon, apricot, pineapple, honey and saffron, sweet and rich, but with a freshness that keeps it lively.

It is on the list as one of the great sweet wines of Bordeaux, and it suits the Lemon Tart because its citrus meets the yuzu and lemon jelly, and its honey loves the toasted meringue.

changes.before:
The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire, and soon passed to Don José Faurie. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the centre of the balcony railing.

From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy many called the unofficial world champion, lived there until his death in 1884.

Brennan's has served here since 1956. Guests often ask how old the building is while they wait for the first course, so point them to the balcony monogram on the way out: it is the easiest way to make the history real.

Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified French restaurant cooking in Le Guide Culinaire, organised sauces into families. The mother sauces are espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise; every other classical sauce is a daughter, built by adding to one of them.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Hussarde and Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou, Foyot on the Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin and bordelaise come from the brown side.

The guide's own advice is that the sauce usually matters more than the protein, for the guest and for the wine. Learn the sauce on each plate first and the rest of the description follows.

Marchand de vin means wine merchant. In classical French cooking it is shallots reduced in red wine with a brown stock or demi-glace. New Orleans made its own version: onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushrooms, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce. Antoine's made it famous in the city.

The guide's best wording is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; calling it a bare reduction undersells it.

On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the dark, winey half of the two sauces, under the egg. Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef before you promise either.

Sauce Choron is béarnaise finished with tomato. It is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the celebrated Voisin restaurant on the rue Saint-Honoré in Paris, who is also remembered for the extraordinary Christmas menu he served during the Siege of Paris.

The tomato is cooked down to a thick paste before it is folded in, so it colours the sauce a soft coral and adds a gentle sweetness without thinning the emulsion.

Brennan's puts Choron on the Eggs Sardou in place of the usual hollandaise. The guide's words for it are tangy and herbal, and that is how to say it to a guest: béarnaise with tomato, brighter than hollandaise.

Sauce Foyot, also called sauce Valois, is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Glace de viande is brown stock reduced until it is thick and syrupy; a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savoury.

It takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot on the rue de Tournon in Paris, opposite the Senate, named for Nicolas Foyot, who had cooked for King Louis-Philippe. Several dishes there carried the house name.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand it does a necessary job: tenderloin is the leanest, mildest cut on the animal, so a rich, savoury sauce brings the depth the meat lacks. Say it as béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze.

Crème anglaise is the French pouring custard: milk or cream heated with sugar and vanilla, poured over egg yolks, and stirred gently until it coats the back of a spoon, never boiled or it curdles. It is the base of ice cream and of a Bavarian cream.

A sweetened condensed anglaise is the kitchen's twist: condensed milk, cooked down with sugar, brings a caramel, dulce de leche note to the custard.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is poured beside the charred pineapple and puff pastry, cool and silky against hot caramel. Say it to a guest as a pouring custard with a caramelised milk flavour.

changes.before:
A roux is flour cooked in fat, stirred constantly, and used to thicken and flavour a sauce or soup. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel and velouté. Louisiana cooks take it much further, to peanut butter, then chocolate or mahogany brown, which gives a toasty, nutty depth; the darker it gets, the more flavour and the less thickening power it has.

A dark roux is the Creole tradition for gumbo and turtle soup, and New Orleans marchand de vin is often roux-bound too. How dark our own kitchen takes each one is a question for the chef.

At the table, a roux is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

The holy trinity is onion, celery and green bell pepper, chopped and softened together at the start of a Cajun or Creole dish. It is Louisiana's version of the French mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, which grew more easily in early Louisiana.

The name nods to the Catholic faith of the early settlers, and the phrase was most likely popularised by the chef Paul Prudhomme. Garlic is so often added that some cooks call it the pope.

The trinity is in our gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana rice dressing. It is the reason those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in.

Grits are dried corn ground coarse and simmered slowly in water or milk until creamy, the Southern answer to polenta. Stone-ground grits keep more of the corn's germ and flavour and take longer to cook than quick grits; hominy grits are made from corn treated with alkali.

They are a blank, comforting base that takes on butter, cheese and sauce.

We serve them two ways: Cheddar Grits as a breakfast side, and a fried pimento cheese grit cake, crisp outside and creamy inside, under the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits. Whether ours are stone-ground, and whose corn, are good questions for the kitchen.

Brennan's makes its own, and the menu names it on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak; the breakfast hanger, the potato on the Eggs Owen and the Roost's spiced nuts are seasoned in the same style.

changes.before:
Brown butter, beurre noisette in French, is butter cooked past melting until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty and sweet. It must be stopped at that moment, often with lemon or vinegar, because a few seconds more and it burns bitter.

That nutty depth is why it appears across our menus in different forms.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid; the spinach in the Turtle Soup is wilted in brown butter; and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle are made with it, which is what makes them taste buttery rather than cakey.

The Baked Apple starts with a whole apple, peeled, cored and trimmed flat so it stands. A crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon is packed on top, and the apple bakes until a skewer slides through with no resistance. The brown sugar melts into the apple's juices and caramelises, which is where the glaze comes from.

It is the French baked apple meeting the British crumble, warm and soft under a little crunch.

It is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast, after the Brandy Milk Punch. Which apple the kitchen uses, and whether the tasting portion is whole or half, are good lineup questions.

Filet mignon is a small steak cut from the narrow end of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That makes it the most tender cut on the animal and also one of the mildest, so it relies on its sauce and garnish for savour.

A petite filet is a small portion that cooks quickly: seared hard, finished gently and rested for a few minutes so the juices settle.

On the Traditional Breakfast it is the fourth course, with a crisp potato rösti, garlic spinach and a 4 oz pour of Côtes du Rhône. Take the guest's temperature when you take the tasting order, not when the course fires.

Garlic spinach is fresh spinach wilted quickly in a hot pan with oil or butter and sliced garlic, then squeezed of its water and seasoned at the last moment so it stays bright green rather than grey.

It is the simplest of the greens on our menus, light where the creamed spinach is rich.

On the Petite Filet Mignon it brings the savour that a mild filet lacks: garlic, iron and a little bitterness to balance the beef and the crisp rösti. If a guest asks how it differs from the Sardou's spinach, the answer is that this one is wilted with garlic, not creamed with Parmesan.

A white bean stew is dried white beans soaked and simmered slowly with aromatics and stock until they are creamy but still whole, the idea behind a French cassoulet or a pot of Louisiana beans. The beans drink up fat and flavour, so they make a soft bed for something rich.

Kept loose and spoonable, the stew catches the sauce from whatever sits on top.

Under the Louisiana BBQ Lobster it carries 'nduja, so the beans are creamy, porky and gently hot, and the buttery BBQ sauce runs into them. Whether the 'nduja is cooked into the beans or added as a finishing spoonful is a good question for the chef.

Rohan is not a breed but a proprietary cross created for D'Artagnan, a specialty meat company. It brings together the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, and the birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York State's Catskills, without antibiotics, to about eleven weeks, longer than most commercial ducks.

The name honours the Rohan family of Brittany. The meat is rosy, tender and milder than wild duck, with a good layer of fat under the skin.

We use it twice: the roasted breast on the dinner tasting and the confit leg on the Duck Confit Waffle. Say a special cross raised in New York, and do not call it a breed.

A duck breast carries a thick layer of fat under the skin, and the cook's job is to render most of it away while keeping the meat rosy. The skin is scored in a tight crosshatch, the breast goes skin-down into a cold or moderate pan, and the fat melts out slowly as the skin crisps. A short turn on the flesh side, a finish in the oven and a rest of a few minutes follow, then it is sliced across the grain.

Duck breast is served pink, like a steak; cooked through it turns grey and livery.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast comes with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The usual doneness is medium-rare to medium; confirm at lineup.

Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles until thick, with nothing taken out. Molasses is what remains after sugar has been crystallised and removed, so cane syrup is sweeter, lighter and milder, with a buttery caramel taste rather than molasses's bitter edge. Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910, after a freeze threatened a cane crop.

It is a Louisiana pantry staple poured on biscuits, baked into cakes and used to glaze meat.

On the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast it glazes peaches, sweet and caramelised against rich duck. The menu does not name a brand, so say Louisiana cane syrup, a lighter cousin of molasses.

A trifle is an English layered pudding with centuries of history: sponge or biscuits soaked in sherry or juice, fruit, custard and whipped cream, built in a glass bowl so the layers show. It was a dish for gatherings and a way to use up cake.

Our Blackberry Trifle rebuilds it in French pastry terms. Fruit curds take the place of custard, small financiers replace the sponge, and a coconut chia pudding is the modern layer.

It is built in a glass so the guest sees the colours. Served as a starter on the breakfast and lunch menu, it suits the middle of the table while the eggs are cooking: tart rather than sugary.

A fruit curd is a cooked spread of fruit juice, sugar, egg yolks and butter, stirred over gentle heat until it thickens to coat a spoon, then chilled until set. Lemon curd is the British classic; blackberry curd uses the purée of the fruit, which gives a deep purple colour and a tart, jammy taste.

Curds are richer and sharper than jam and silkier than custard.

In the Blackberry Trifle the two curds are the bright, tart layers, purple and yellow, that keep the dessert from tasting sugary. They are made ahead and set cold, so the trifle can be built quickly to order. The service note lists what the curds contain.

A financier is a small French cake of ground almonds, egg whites, sugar, a little flour and brown butter, baked in a small mould. The standard account credits a Paris pâtissier named Lasne, whose shop stood near the stock exchange around 1890; he shaped them like little gold bars for the traders, and the name stuck.

The brown butter is what makes them taste rich and nutty, with crisp edges and a moist centre.

In the Blackberry Trifle they are blackberry financier biscuits, the trifle's answer to sponge. The guide notes they are traditionally made with almond flour and asks you to confirm with the kitchen.

French toast is pain perdu, lost bread: stale bread rescued by soaking it in egg and milk, often with sugar and vanilla, and frying it in butter. In New Orleans it is an old Creole breakfast. The bread must be thick and slightly dry, or it soaks to mush; the pan must be moderate, so the custard centre sets before the outside burns.

Brioche makes the richest version, soft and custardy inside with a caramelised crust.

Our Framboise French Toast uses housemade citrus brioche, sold as a starter to share, and the children's breakfast offers a vanilla French toast with berries and whipped cream.

Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming after-dinner coffee. Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with cinnamon, clove and a long spiral of orange and lemon peel, then ladled into strong coffee at the table. Brûlot comes from brûler, to burn.

It is one of the city's great tableside rituals.

Brennan's borrows its flavours for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. The drink itself is not on our list, so sell the cake as the coffee's flavours, not the flame.

Grand Isle is the barrier island at the edge of the Louisiana coast. Grand Isle Jewels is a brand launched in April 2025 by JEDCO, the Jefferson Parish economic development commission, with the island's off-bottom oyster farmers.

Off-bottom farming raises oysters in cages that float or hang above the seafloor. The cages float just below the surface in an aquapark where ocean and estuary water mix, which keeps the oysters off the mud and gives them a briny, bright flavour, and the method is gentler on a storm-damaged coast than dredging wild reefs.

We serve them raw with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette, at dinner and as the first course of the dinner tasting. Know the count per order, and ask the chef whether to tell the farming story.

Bottarga is salted, pressed and dried fish roe, grey mullet in Sardinia and tuna in Sicily, grated over pasta like a savoury cheese. Egg yolk bottarga borrows the idea: yolks are buried in salt and sugar for a day or more, rinsed and dried at low heat until firm enough to grate.

On the Steak Tartare Cannoli it is grated over the top in place of the raw yolk of a classic tartare. It is the only dish on the current menus with it, so do not describe cured yolk as a standing house preparation.

The turtle in our soup is snapping turtle, a freshwater turtle. The wild alligator snapper has been off limits to commercial trappers in Louisiana since 2004, so restaurants buy it from licensed turtle farms, or buy common snapping turtle, which licensed collectors may still sell. The meat is dark, firm and rich, somewhere between veal and dark chicken, with plenty of gelatine, which gives the soup its body.

It is chopped finely and simmered for a long time, so it is tender and spread through the soup rather than served in chunks.

When a guest hesitates, describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep beef stew. The current supplier is a question for the chef, not a guess.

Canadian bacon is cured, lightly smoked pork loin, lean and ham-like, sliced into rounds; it is the meat of Eggs Benedict. A coffee cure rubs the loin with salt, sugar and ground coffee before it is smoked or roasted, adding a roasty, slightly bitter depth to the sweet, salty pork.

What can be said is how the plate relates to its neighbours. It takes the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, and replaces the Canadian bacon and muffin with red wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, topped with a soft-boiled egg.

It is the heartier choice at $32 against the Hussarde at $27: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

Braising cooks a tough, well-worked cut slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, so its connective tissue melts into gelatin. Short rib is ideal: marbled, sinewy and full of flavour.

The ribs are seared hard for colour, the vegetables sweated, the pan deglazed with red wine and reduced, then stock added; the pot goes into a low oven for about three hours, until a fork turns the meat. The liquid is skimmed and reduced into a glossy sauce, and the meat is pulled back into it.

That is the short rib débris on the Eggs Owen: meltingly tender beef in a deep, winey gravy, which echoes the marchand de vin on the same plate.

An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan. The French omelette is stirred as it sets, then rolled into a smooth, pale cylinder with a soft, creamy centre and barely any colour. The American omelette is set flat, filled, and folded in half, firmer and lightly golden.

Either way the filling goes in warm, so the eggs are not overcooked waiting for it.

An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan. The French omelette is stirred as it sets, then rolled into a smooth, pale cylinder with a soft, creamy center and barely any color. The American omelette is set flat, filled, and folded in half, firmer and lightly golden.

Either way the filling goes in warm, so the eggs are not overcooked waiting for it.

Miso is a Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji, a mould grown on rice or barley. White miso is mild and sweet; darker misos are saltier and stronger. Beaten into soft butter, it makes a compound butter that is salty, nutty and deeply savoury.

It brings umami, the savoury depth of aged cheese and cured ham, without tasting obviously Japanese.

On the Crab & Corn Omelette the house-made miso butter rounds out the sweet crab and corn. The guide names soy from the miso on this dish, so send dietary questions to the service note and the kitchen.

The hanger steak, onglet in France, hangs from the diaphragm near the kidneys. There is only one per animal, which is why butchers used to keep it for themselves and why it was long called the butcher's steak. A tough sinew runs down its centre and is cut out, leaving two loose-grained lobes.

It is intensely beefy and best cooked hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, rested, and sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver.

We serve two: the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch with béarnaise and an egg, and the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner with chilli crisp. Always take the temperature.

Hens that forage outdoors often lay eggs with deep orange yolks, and a sunny-side-up egg shows that colour off.

Sautéing cooks food quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan. For a fish fillet, the pan and fat are hot before it goes in, often skin or presentation side first; it is left alone to colour, then turned once and finished gently so it stays moist and flakes at the touch. Many kitchens dust the fillet with flour first, the meunière way, for a golden crust.

Thin, delicate fish cook in two or three minutes; thicker fillets are finished in the oven.

The children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked this way, and the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapour burns in a burst of blue and orange flame. It is theatre and flavour at once, caramelising the sauce's surface. At Brennan's it is done on a guéridon, the tableside cart.

The guide's steps are learned word for word: measure the spirit into a small vessel, never pour from the bottle near a flame, pull the pan off the flame to add it, tilt to ignite, keep a lid in reach, let the flame die before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving.

In a bright breakfast room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it clearly has died down.

Gentle heat is everything: too hot and the eggs curdle into a grainy, weeping custard.

In The Snickers it plays the caramel layer of the candy bar, silky and toasty against the milk chocolate Bavarian cream, the nougat ice cream and the salty roasted peanuts. If a guest asks, it is the soft caramel part of the bar.

Nougat is a confection of honey and sugar whipped into egg whites, usually studded with nuts, almonds, pistachios or hazelnuts; soft nougat is the chewy centre of many candy bars. As an ice cream it tastes of honey, toasted nuts and vanilla.

It is the frozen version of the candy bar's nougat layer.

In The Snickers it sits with roasted peanuts, caramel custard and milk chocolate Bavarian cream. Classic nougat often carries tree nuts besides the dish's peanuts, so ask the kitchen what is in it for any guest with a nut question.

The French tarte au citron is sweet pastry filled with a sharp lemon curd, often crowned with meringue. Our Lemon Tart takes it apart: the pastry becomes a sweet pastry crumb, the curd becomes a light yuzu mousse, the sharpness is concentrated in a lemon jelly, and the meringue is piped and toasted.

The deconstruction keeps the flavours and makes the whole dessert lighter.

It is $14 and the lightest dessert on the list. The guide names it, with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, as the dessert to steer to for guests who avoid alcohol, since the flamed desserts and the bread pudding all carry spirits.

Its zest and juice perfume a dish far beyond their quantity.

Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart: fruit caramelised in butter and sugar in a pan, covered with pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry is underneath. It is named for Stéphanie and Caroline Tatin, who ran the Hôtel Tatin at Lamotte-Beuvron in the Sologne. The story of an accident with overcooked apples is a legend; the region already made such tarts, and Maxim's in Paris made the name famous.

Apples are classic. Pineapple is wetter and needs more browning, hence charred.

Our Pineapple Tarte Tatin is $14 with puff pastry, sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse, and a dessert without spirits.

Cheddar takes its name from the English village of Cheddar, and is now made all over the world. Its curds are cut, stacked and turned, a process called cheddaring, which presses out whey and gives the cheese its dense, smooth texture. Sharp cheddar melts well and holds its flavour in a sauce.

The title is wistful, a look back at how things seemed, and the drink sits under Temperance, 1946, the spirit-free list.

It is the twin of Old Buttermilk Sky: Lyre's non-alcoholic agave spirit with fig syrup, lemon, cinnamon syrup and egg white, a silky sour without spirit. Because Lyre's is labelled under 0.5 percent alcohol, a server says non-alcoholic, never alcohol free.

Spirit-free drinks need exact words, because guests who avoid alcohol rely on them. Zero proof is a marketing term, not a legal one and not a guarantee of 0.0; some zero proof products carry a trace. Non-alcoholic, in American labelling, allows under 0.5 percent.

The two drinks under Temperance, 1946 show the difference. Personality is built on Wölffer Estate's zero proof sparkling rosé; confirm the figure on its label at lineup. Oh! What It Seemed to Be is built on Lyre's agave, which Lyre's labels under 0.5 percent, so a server says non-alcoholic, never alcohol free or zero.

Each has a spirited twin on the fall list, Rumors are Flying and Old Buttermilk Sky, so a whole table can share an idea. Any question about pregnancy, medication or recovery is answered with the label and the bar, never a promise from the server.

In the classic Sazerac build two glasses are used: one is packed with ice to chill while the drink is stirred in the other. The serving glass is emptied, coated with the anise spirit and drained, and the stirred drink is strained into it, with no ice.

At Brennan's the Classic is rinsed with Herbsaint and Thompson's Dream with St. George absinthe; the Origin Story carries Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe in the same pattern. The bar confirms its own steps.

A dry shake is a shake without ice, used for drinks with egg white. Shaken warm, the egg white's proteins unfold and trap air, whipping into a foam rather like a soft meringue. The bartender then adds ice and shakes again to chill and dilute. In the reverse dry shake the order is swapped, ice first, then a shake without it.

The result is the pale, velvety cap on a sour and the silky body under it; the egg white adds texture, not flavour.

Two Brennan's drinks print egg white: Old Buttermilk Sky and its spirit-free twin, Oh! What It Seemed to Be. The menu prints no method, so the dry shake is the classic technique and the bar confirms its build. Any question about egg goes to the service note and lineup.

changes.before:
Barrel ageing means resting a spirit, a finished cocktail or even bitters in an oak cask. The wood softens sharp edges and adds vanilla, caramel and spice, and a little evaporation concentrates what is left. A used spirit cask lends some of its old contents too.

Two Brennan's drinks print it. Rumors are Flying is built on Brennan's Barrel Aged Rittenhouse Rye, and the Origin Story uses barrel-aged Peychaud's.

What the menu does not print is who did the ageing, in what cask and for how long. Those are questions for the bar, so a server says barrel-aged for Brennan's and no more until the bar gives the story. Guests often ask; it is worth asking at lineup. The Sazerac Company does sell a Peychaud's Barrel-Aged; whether ours is that bottle is a question for the bar.

Cold pressing is a way of making juice without heat or fast spinning blades. The fruit is ground to a pulp and pressed hard, often in a cloth, so the juice is squeezed out slowly and stays cool.

Juice made this way keeps more of the fresh fruit's colour and bright flavour; because it is not pasteurised by heat, it is usually kept cold and has a short life.

The Revive Cold-Pressed Juice is listed under juices that are locally made and fresh squeezed: strawberry, apple and pineapple. Who presses it for Brennan's is not printed, and a search could not confirm the maker, so that is a question for the bar. It is the drink for a guest who wants neither alcohol nor caffeine.

A real bean gives a deeper, more floral and warmer perfume than extract. In a bar it is usually steeped ahead in the cream or a syrup, so the flavour is ready for every shake.

The menu prints vanilla bean, not extract, for the Brandy Milk Punch, and a server can say so with pride; how the bar uses the bean is a question for lineup. Vanilla is also the backbone of the housemade vanilla bean ice cream in Floating in South Africa, and Licor 43 in Five Minutes More leans on it.

Vodka is a neutral spirit distilled to high strength from grain, potatoes or other starches, then filtered and cut with water. It is meant to be clean, with little taste of its own beyond a soft texture and a hint of the grain or potato.

That cleanness is its job in a cocktail: it carries other flavours without fighting them, which is why it anchors the Bloody Mary and the espresso martini.

At Brennan's the menus name a brand only in some drinks. The Bloody Bull, the Bloody Mary and the Espresso Martini print vodka alone, so which vodka is a question for the bar. The Flamingo names Chopin, a Polish potato vodka, and Five Minutes More names Cathead's mandarin vodka from Mississippi.

Bouillon is French for broth: a clear, savoury stock made by simmering beef, bones and vegetables, strained clean. Cold beef bouillon has a rich, meaty depth with no fat on it.

In a drink it turns a Bloody Mary into something closer to a spicy, chilled consommé, which is how the guide describes the Bloody Bull. The idea comes from the Bull Shot of 1952, vodka and canned beef bouillon.

At Brennan's it is the reason the Bloody Bull pours with the turtle soup on the Traditional Breakfast. It also means the drink carries beef: the guide's service note says so plainly and offers the Brennan's Bloody Mary instead. Whether the bouillon is a house stock is a question for the bar.

Herbsaint is New Orleans' own anise liqueur. J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learned absinthe making in France during the First World War, created it in New Orleans in 1934, after Prohibition and while absinthe was banned. It was sold first as Legendre Absinthe, though it held no grand wormwood; the federal authorities objected, and it became Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole name for wormwood.

It is built on brandy and flavoured with wormwood, star anise and fennel, then coloured and perfumed with herbs such as lemon balm, hyssop, meadowsweet, basil, mint, tarragon and stinging nettle. At 60 percent alcohol it is herbal and green rather than candied.

Chicory is a hardy plant whose root is dried, roasted and ground. Brewed with coffee it adds body, a dark colour and a roasty, cocoa-like bitterness, and it carries no caffeine of its own.

The French used it to stretch coffee during Napoleon's blockade, and New Orleans, a French city and a great coffee port, kept the habit; the Civil War blockade is said to have fixed it.

Chicory runs through the Brennan's coffee list. The New Orleans-style coffee is blended with it, the Irish Coffee and the walnut and hazelnut coffee use the dark roast with chicory, the Café Glacé is chicory cold brew, and the Espresso Martini prints chicory. How it goes into the martini is a question for the bar.

Brown sugar is sugar that keeps some of its molasses, which gives it a soft, caramel and toffee flavour and a darker colour than white sugar. Dissolved with water it becomes brown sugar syrup, the bar's easy way to sweeten a cold drink.

In hot coffee it melts straight in; in cold drinks a syrup is used, because grains do not dissolve in the cold.

Its Brut La Française is the non-vintage house style, unusual for its high share of Chardonnay, about 40 percent, with Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, aged close to four years on the lees in the chalk cellars under Reims.

In the Flamingo it tops Chopin vodka, Monkey 47 gin, dragonfruit and lemon. Brennan's also lists Taittinger La Française as a 3 litre double magnum on the Birthday Bubbles list, so the name links the Roost cocktail to the cellar.

Hendrick's is a Scottish gin launched in 1999 by William Grant and Sons at Girvan. It is made in two stills of different design whose spirits are blended, and essences of Bulgarian rose and cucumber are added after distillation.

That cucumber and rose made it stand apart when it launched, and they give it a cool, fresh, floral character, softer than a classic juniper-led gin.

In the Spoonbill it meets Cap Corse Mattei Blanc quinquina and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar alongside. The cucumber links naturally to the green chive, and the rose to the aperitif wine, which is a neat way to explain why the drink tastes so cool and savoury.

Louis-Napoléon Mattei opened his house in Bastia in 1872 and made his first quinquina wine in 1875; the aperitif is named for Cap Corse, the northern peninsula of Corsica. The house page prints it as Cap Corse Mattei Blanc Quinquina vermouth; strictly it is a quinquina, a cousin of vermouth. In the Spoonbill it plays the vermouth's part in a martini-style drink with Hendrick's gin and chive oil, with a spoon of caviar served alongside.

Good caviar tastes clean and briny, buttery and nutty, and the eggs pop softly on the tongue. It is served cold, traditionally on a non-metal spoon of mother of pearl or horn.

The Spoonbill comes with a spoon of caviar alongside, which makes the drink a moment. Which caviar, how much and how it is presented are confirmed with the bar; any question about fish or roe goes to the service note and lineup.

Earl Grey is black tea scented with oil of bergamot, a fragrant citrus grown mostly in Calabria in southern Italy. It is named for Charles Grey, the second Earl Grey, Prime Minister from 1830 to 1834; the stories of how the blend got his name are uncertain, so tell them lightly if at all.

Bergamot gives the tea a floral, perfumed citrus note over the tannic black tea.

Riesling is Germany's great white grape, and many sommeliers' favourite. It ripens slowly in cool, steep vineyards, keeps a high, racy acidity and gives intense aromas of green apple, lime, peach and, from slate soils, a stony edge; with age it gains honey and a note sommeliers call petrol.

It is made at every level of sweetness, from bone dry to lusciously sweet, and that acidity keeps even the sweetest from tasting heavy. Low alcohol is common in the Mosel.

Our list is unusually rich in it: the off-dry Berres by the glass, Prüm, Egon Müller, Dönnhoff and Keller from Germany, Bründlmayer's dry Heiligenstein from Austria. Its touch of sweetness and acidity make it the classic answer to spice, smoke and the maple on the duck.

On our list it appears in Whispering Angel, the Tempier Bandol rosé and the Saint Damien Gigondas. A server rarely needs to sell Cinsault by name, but knowing it explains why these rosés are so delicate.

changes.before:
Cabernet Sauvignon is the red grape of Bordeaux's Left Bank and of Napa Valley. Small, thick-skinned berries give deep colour, firm tannin and flavours of blackcurrant, cedar, tobacco and graphite, with a fresh, structured frame that ages for decades.

It is born of a chance crossing of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, and in Bordeaux it is blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot. In California it is often bottled almost alone.

Ours run from the Moulin d'Issan by the glass and the dinner tasting's Paul Hobbs Coombsville to Inglenook Rubicon, Ridge's mountain Estate, Duckhorn and the Pauillac and Saint-Julien growths. Its tannin loves fat and protein: filet, Chateaubriand and hanger steak.

Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape. It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon and gives rounder, plusher wine: plum, black cherry, cocoa and soft tannin.

On the Right Bank, in Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, it leads the blend on clay and limestone. On the Left Bank it fills out Cabernet Sauvignon, and Pichon Lalande is known for using more of it than its Pauillac neighbours. In California Duckhorn first made its name with Merlot.

On our list it is in the Moulin d'Issan, Troplong Mondot, the Médoc growths, Inglenook Rubicon and Duckhorn's Cabernet. For a guest who wants red but finds Cabernet too firm, a Merlot-led Saint-Émilion is the gentle step.

Petite Sirah and Carignane are the two partners Zinfandel grew up with in California's old vineyards. Petite Sirah, a cross of Syrah and an old French grape called Peloursin, is inky and tannic, with blueberry and black pepper. Carignane, Carignan in France, adds bright acidity, red fruit and a rustic spice.

Early growers planted them side by side with Zinfandel as a field blend, picked and fermented together, so the wine was balanced in the vineyard rather than in the cellar. Ridge keeps that tradition, naming each grape on the label.

They give the Ridge Lytton Springs and Three Valleys their colour, grip and freshness. When a guest asks why the bottle says Lytton Springs rather than Zinfandel, the share of each grape changes with the vintage, so the back label or the sommelier has the answer.

Tempranillo is Spain's great red grape; its name comes from temprano, early, because it ripens early. In Rioja it gives medium-bodied wine with red cherry, strawberry, tobacco and leather and moderate tannin, and it takes well to long barrel ageing.

Graciano is a small, aromatic partner, deep in colour and high in acidity, used in a few parts in ten to lift the blend and help it age.

Our La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 is about nine parts Tempranillo to one of Graciano, aged about four years in American oak, which adds vanilla, coconut and sweet spice. It is a mellow, savoury red for lamb, duck and roast meats, and a good bottle for a guest who loves old-style wine.

Sémillon is a golden-skinned white grape from Bordeaux. Its thin skins make it prone to botrytis, the noble rot that shrivels grapes in autumn mists, and that is what makes it the heart of Sauternes and Barsac.

It gives weight, a waxy, honeyed texture and flavours of apricot, lemon and saffron, while a little Sauvignon Blanc usually adds acidity and perfume. Château Climens is unusual in using Sémillon alone.

Every Sauternes and Barsac on our list is Sémillon-led: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens and Gilette. With age it turns amber and tastes of crème brûlée and marmalade, which is why it flatters the Bread Pudding and the Bananas Foster.

Melon de Bourgogne is the grape of Muscadet, near Nantes, where the Loire meets the Atlantic. As its name says, it came from Burgundy; after a hard frost destroyed the vineyards of the region, growers replanted with this frost-hardy vine.

On its own it is light and neutral, with lemon, green apple and a salty, oyster-shell finish. Growers give it more by leaving it on its lees, the spent yeast, for months or years, which adds texture and a bready, savoury depth.

Our two, from Domaine de l'Écu and Domaine de la Pépière, are serious Muscadet, aged long on the lees. They are the classic wine with raw oysters, and with the Grand Isle Jewels they are hard to beat.

Pinot Gris is a pink-grey skinned mutation of Pinot Noir. In Italy it is Pinot Grigio, made light and crisp; in Alsace it is a different animal: rich, full and spicy, with ripe pear, quince, honey and a smoky note.

Alsace growers often pick it very ripe, so some bottles carry a touch of sweetness and others are dry; the label does not always say, so the sommelier is the one to ask. It ages well, gaining dried apricot, ginger and mushroom.

We have Albert Boxler's and Trimbach's Réserve Personnelle 2007. Its weight and spice handle rich, smoky dishes, duck and foie gras.

Assyrtiko is the great white grape of Santorini. It keeps very high acidity even in the hot, dry Aegean summer, which is rare, and gives bone dry wine tasting of lemon, salt, flint and white flowers.

On Santorini the vines grow in volcanic pumice that phylloxera never reached, so many are ungrafted and very old, trained low into basket shapes against the wind. The result has a savoury, almost salty depth.

Ours is Gaia's Wild Ferment, fermented with the island's own yeasts. Sell it as the white for grilled fish, lemon and herbs, and for any guest who loves Chablis or Sancerre.

Savagnin is an ancient white grape of the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland. It is related to Traminer, the parent of Gewürztraminer, but it is not aromatic in the same way: it is firm, high in acidity and savoury.

It is the only grape allowed in Vin Jaune, the yellow wine, which ages for years in barrel under a veil of yeast and tastes of walnut, curry spice and dried apple.

Ours is the Domaine du Pélican Vin Jaune from Arbois. It is a curiosity for adventurous guests, and a famous match for aged Comté cheese, mushrooms and chicken in cream.

Marsanne and Roussanne are the white grapes of the Rhône. Marsanne gives body, a waxy texture and flavours of almond, pear and honey; Roussanne adds perfume, herbs and freshness. Grenache Blanc and Clairette, two southern whites, add roundness and floral lift.

Together they make full, textured whites that age well, gaining honey and fennel notes, and they suit rich fish and poultry far better than crisp, lean wines do.

Our example is the rare white of Domaine de Trévallon in the Alpilles, Marsanne-led with Roussanne, a little Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Clairette. It is a bottle for a guest who loves white Burgundy and wants something rarer.

Palomino is the white grape of sherry, grown on the bright white albariza chalk around Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda in southern Spain.

As a table wine it is neutral and low in acidity, which is exactly why it suits sherry: it lets the ageing speak. Under a layer of flor yeast it becomes fino or, in the sea air of Sanlúcar, Manzanilla, tasting of green apple, almond, bread dough and salt.

Ours is La Cigarrera Manzanilla in a half-bottle. Serve it well chilled as an aperitif; it is a bold, classic match for oysters, fried seafood and salty snacks.

Corvina is the main red grape of Valpolicella, in the hills north of Verona, usually blended with Corvinone and Rondinella. On its own it gives light, cherry-scented red with bright acidity.

Its thick skins are what matter: the grapes can be dried for months after picking without rotting, losing water and concentrating sugar, colour and flavour. That process, appassimento, makes dry Amarone and sweet Recioto.

Our bottle is Giuseppe Quintarelli's Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997, from Corvina, Corvinone, Rondinella and other local grapes. With chocolate and the richer desserts it is a rare treat.

Malvasia, Malmsey in English, is an ancient family of grapes found all around the Mediterranean. On the Portuguese island of Madeira it gives the sweetest of the four classic styles, named for the grape.

A Malvasia Madeira must carry a lot of sugar, yet the island's high natural acidity keeps it tangy and alive. Warm ageing in old casks turns it amber and gives coffee, caramel, toffee, orange peel, dried fig and walnut.

Ours is the Broadbent Single Cask Malvasia 2009, in a 500 ml bottle. Opened, Madeira lasts longer than almost any wine. Offer it with the Bread Pudding, nuts and coffee desserts.

Port is made from a field of native Portuguese red grapes grown on the steep schist terraces of the Douro valley. The five most prized are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Spain's Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão; old vineyards mix dozens together.

Touriga Nacional gives floral violet aromas, deep colour and firm tannin; Touriga Franca adds perfume and red fruit; Tinta Roriz brings body. The blend is why Port can taste of blackberry, plum, violets and dark chocolate at once.

Every Port on our list, from Dow's and Graham's to Taylor Fladgate, Niepoort, Sandeman and Feist, is a blend of these grapes. Most bottles do not name them, so a guest who asks gets the family, not a recipe.

The Montagne de Reims is the wooded hill between Reims and Épernay, more a plateau than a mountain, ringed with vineyards. It is Pinot Noir country, and its Grand Cru villages, Bouzy, Ambonnay, Verzenay and others, give Champagne power, red-fruit depth and structure.

Bouzy is also famous for still red wine, a little of which is blended into rosé Champagne to give it colour. Tauxières is a Premier Cru village on its southern slope; Merfy lies on the smaller hills north-west of Reims.

On our list the Montagne speaks through Paul Bara's Grand Cru rosé and Pierre Paillard's Les Parcelles, both from Bouzy, through Chartogne-Taillet of Merfy and Bollinger's PNTX20, led by Tauxières. Say Pinot Noir, body and red fruit.

The Vallée de la Marne follows the river west from Épernay. Its cooler, frost-prone slopes suit Meunier, while Aÿ, on the north bank near Épernay, is one of Champagne's most famous Grand Cru villages for Pinot Noir.

Aÿ has been a wine town for centuries and is home to Bollinger. Its neighbour Mareuil-sur-Aÿ is home to Billecart-Salmon, and Tours-sur-Marne, a little upstream, to Laurent-Perrier.

So three of our great houses sit within a few miles of one another on the Marne. When a guest asks where Bollinger comes from, the answer is Aÿ, the Pinot Noir village, and it explains the house's rich, powerful style.

The Loire is France's longest river, and its vineyards follow it for hundreds of miles, from Sancerre in the centre of France to Muscadet near the Atlantic at Nantes. It is a cool region of crisp, fresh wines, many of them unoaked.

Each stretch has its own grape: Sauvignon Blanc upstream in Sancerre; Chenin Blanc in the middle, around Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou; Cabernet Franc for reds; Melon de Bourgogne for Muscadet by the sea.

Our Loire bottles show the range: the Durand Sauvignon by the glass, Cotat's Sancerre and Chavignol rosé, Huet's Vouvray in three sweetness levels, Laureau's Savennières, the Baumard Layon and two serious Muscadet bottles. Loire wines, high in acidity, suit seafood and light dishes.

Chablis is the northernmost part of Burgundy, nearer Champagne than Beaune, and it makes only Chardonnay. Its cool climate and Kimmeridgian soil, limestone and clay full of fossilised oyster shells, give lean, crisp, steely wines that taste of lemon, green apple and a chalky, oyster-shell finish.

The tiers run Petit Chablis, Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. The seven Grand Crus, Les Preuses among them, sit on one slope facing south-west across the little Serein river.

We have Louis Michel's village Chablis and Montmains Premier Cru, made in steel with no oak, and Dauvissat's Les Preuses Grand Cru. Chablis with oysters is the oldest pairing advice there is.

Meursault is the largest white wine village of the Côte de Beaune, and its Chardonnay is the richest of the great three: round, nutty and buttery, with hazelnut, ripe lemon, toast and a stony freshness underneath, usually from fermentation and ageing in oak barrels.

It has no Grand Cru, but famous Premier Crus such as Perrières, Charmes and Genevrières, and many named village vineyards, lieux-dits, like Les Tillets, Les Corbins and the Clos de la Baronne. Every November the village holds the Paulée de Meursault, a harvest feast.

Our list carries Meursault from Jadot, Dupont-Fahn, Bitouzet-Prieur, Comtes Lafon and Leflaive's Sous le Dos d'Ane. For a guest who wants a rich, classic white with lobster or crab, this is the page.

Puligny-Montrachet is the most famous white wine village in the world. It shares with Chassagne the Grand Cru Le Montrachet, and its own Grand Crus and Premier Crus give Chardonnay that is elegant, floral and chiselled: citrus, white flowers, hazelnut and a fine, chalky tension.

The water table is high here, so cellars are shallow and wines are often aged above ground. Saint-Aubin, tucked into the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, makes wines in a similar style at a gentler price.

We have village Puligny from François Carillon and Domaine Leflaive, and Paul Pillot's Le Charmois Saint-Aubin Premier Cru. Recommend Saint-Aubin to a guest who loves Puligny but wants value.

The water table is high here, so cellars are shallow and wines are often aged above ground. Saint-Aubin, tucked into the hills behind Puligny and Chassagne, makes wines in a similar style at a gentler price.

We have village Puligny from François Carillon and Domaine Leflaive, and Paul Pillot's Le Charmois Saint-Aubin Premier Cru. Recommend Saint-Aubin to a guest who loves Puligny but wants value.

changes.before:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the town that gives the Côte de Nuits its name. Its Pinot Noir is the sturdiest of the Côte: dark cherry and plum, earth, an iron or gamey note and firm tannin for Burgundy, needing a few years to soften.

It has no Grand Cru but many Premier Crus, including Les Saint-Georges and Les Pruliers on the south side of the town. The town is also a centre of the Burgundy trade, home to houses such as Faiveley.

We pour Henri Gouges, the reference name of the village, in a village half-bottle and Les Pruliers Premier Cru, and Grivot's Les Charmois. With the filet, the short rib or game, a Nuits-Saint-Georges is the Burgundy with the backbone.

Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise are neighbouring villages under the Dentelles de Montmirail, a jagged limestone ridge whose name means the lace of Montmirail.

Gigondas makes powerful, Grenache-led reds with Syrah and Mourvèdre, from terraces rising up the slopes: ripe red and black cherry, garrigue, pepper and firm tannin, often called a junior Châteauneuf. Beaumes-de-Venise is famous for its sweet Muscat, but its dry red, Grenache and Syrah, is lighter and juicy.

We pour Domaine de Durban's red by the glass, and Gigondas from Raspail-Ay in a half-bottle and Saint Damien's La Louisianne. Say: the value step to Châteauneuf.

Provence, between the Rhône and the Riviera, has made wine since ancient Greek settlers founded Marseille, and today it is the world's reference for pale, dry rosé. Côtes de Provence is its largest appellation.

The wines are mostly Grenache with Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre and Rolle, Vermentino in Italy, a white grape that adds freshness. The palest colour comes from pressing the grapes gently and quickly, so the juice barely touches the skins.

Our two are Minuty Prestige by the glass, from above the Gulf of Saint-Tropez, and Whispering Angel by the bottle. Peach, strawberry and citrus, dry and light: rosé for the courtyard and for Gulf seafood.

Bandol is a small appellation on the Provençal coast between Marseille and Toulon, with terraced slopes in an amphitheatre facing the sea. It is the home of Mourvèdre, which needs this heat and sea light to ripen.

Its reds must be at least half Mourvèdre and are aged at least eighteen months in wood, dark, gamey and long-lived. Its rosé, Mourvèdre with Grenache and Cinsault, is the most serious in Provence: salmon-pink, savoury and structured, with garrigue and blood orange.

Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier helped make Bandol its own appellation in 1941. We pour the Tempier Bandol rosé, the rosé for a guest who wants pink with real substance.

Roussillon is French Catalonia, the hot corner of France against the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean, near Perpignan. It is famous for vins doux naturels, sweet wines fortified during fermentation.

Banyuls comes from steep schist terraces above the fishing port of Banyuls-sur-Mer; it must be at least half Grenache noir. Rivesaltes, from the plain and hills further north, uses Grenache in its three colours and Muscat. Both may age for decades in old casks, often in the sun, turning amber and nutty.

We pour the La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva with the dinner tasting's dessert, and the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 is on the list: fifty-one years in wood.

changes.before:
The Jura is a small, cool, hilly region between Burgundy and Switzerland, with its own grapes and traditions. Arbois is its main wine town, and it is also where Louis Pasteur grew up and did his research on fermentation.

Its whites, from Chardonnay and Savagnin, are made either topped up in the usual way or deliberately left under a veil of yeast, which gives a nutty, savoury, sherry-like tang. The most famous is Vin Jaune, which ages over six years and is sold in a squat 62 cl bottle, the clavelin.

Domaine du Pélican is the Arbois estate founded by the d'Angerville family of Volnay. Our bottle is its Vin Jaune 2016.

Pauillac is the most famous village of the Médoc, home to three of the five first growths, Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild. Its deep gravel ridges give the most powerful, long-lived Cabernet Sauvignon in Bordeaux: blackcurrant, cedar, cigar box and graphite, with firm tannin.

Classic Pauillac smells of what the British trade calls cigar box and pencil shavings, and with age it softens into a long, savoury finish.

We have two: Château Pichon Lalande, a second growth across the road from Latour, with more Merlot than its neighbours, and Grand-Puy-Lacoste, a fifth growth often called one of the best values in the Médoc. With the Chateaubriand, a mature Pauillac is the textbook pairing.

The Right Bank lies east of the Dordogne river, around the medieval hill town of Saint-Émilion and its neighbour Pomerol. Here the soils are clay and limestone, cooler than the Médoc's gravel, and Merlot leads with Cabernet Franc.

The wines are plusher and rounder than the Left Bank's: plum, black cherry, cocoa and a fresh limestone edge, with finer tannin. Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised about every ten years, unlike the fixed 1855 list.

Our bottle is Château Troplong Mondot, on one of the highest points of the Saint-Émilion plateau, in a half-bottle from 2020. Offer it to a guest who wants red Bordeaux that is generous and soft.

The Mosel winds through western Germany from the French border to the Rhine at Koblenz, its vineyards on some of the steepest slopes in Europe. The slate soil, blue or red, holds the sun's warmth and gives Riesling a stony, mineral edge.

Mosel Riesling is light, often only 8 to 11 per cent alcohol, with racy acidity and green apple, peach and lime, made from dry to lusciously sweet. The famous villages of the Middle Mosel, Ürzig, Erden and Wehlen, face the sun across the river; the Saar, a cooler tributary, gives the steeliest wines of all, at the Scharzhofberg.

Our Mosel bottles include the Berres and Dr. Hermann by the glass, Stein, Prüm and Egon Müller.

Rioja is Spain's most famous red wine region, along the Ebro river in the north. Rioja Alta, the higher, cooler western part, gives its most elegant wines, and the town of Haro is its historic centre, with a cluster of great bodegas in the Barrio de la Estación, the station quarter, built beside the railway in the late nineteenth century to ship wine to France and beyond.

Rioja is defined by Tempranillo and by ageing: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva mark longer times in barrel and bottle, traditionally American oak.

La Rioja Alta S.A., founded in the station quarter in 1890, makes our Gran Reserva 904.

The Santa Cruz Mountains run along the coast south of San Francisco, with vineyards high on ridges above the fog, some over two thousand feet up. Cool nights, thin soils and fractured limestone give Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay with freshness and structure rather than plush ripeness.

Ridge Vineyards' Monte Bello estate sits near the top of one ridge. Its 1971 Cabernet came fifth among the reds at the Paris tasting of 1976 and won the thirtieth anniversary re-tasting outright in 2006.

Our Ridge Estate Cabernet comes from vineyards around Monte Bello: blackcurrant, cedar and graphite, structured and savoury, in a half-bottle.

changes.before:
Dosage is the small dose of wine and sugar added to a sparkling wine just before the final cork, after disgorging. It balances the high acidity, and it decides the word on the label.

From driest to sweetest: Brut Nature, no sugar added; Extra Brut, up to 6 grams a litre; Brut, up to 12; then Extra Dry, 12 to 17; Sec, 17 to 32; and Demi-Sec, 32 to 50 grams, noticeably sweet. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Pommery's Nature of 1874 helped turn the world towards dry Champagne, when much of it was very sweet.

Our house Brennan's Essential is Extra Brut, very dry; most of the list is Brut; the Moët Nectar Impérial Rosé and Laurent-Perrier Harmony are Demi-Sec, for dessert.

changes.before:
A vintage Champagne is made from the grapes of a single year, printed on the label, and houses make one only when the harvest is good enough to stand alone, usually a few times a decade. It must age at least three years before release, and the great ones far longer.

A vintage wine shows the character of its year: the warmth of 2009, the freshness of 2013. Prestige cuvées, such as Rare and Billecart-Salmon's Elisabeth Salmon rosé, are usually vintage wines from the best vineyards with long ageing.

On our list: Rare 2012 by the glass and Rare 2013 by the bottle, Pol Roger Blanc de Blancs 2015, Billecart's Elisabeth Salmon 2009, and from elsewhere Argyle 2022 and Schramsberg's Blanc de Blancs 2021. Always read the vintage on the label.

changes.before:
Rosé Champagne is the only French wine allowed to be made pink by blending red and white wine. Most houses add a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir from villages such as Bouzy or Aÿ, to the white base before the second fermentation, which gives a reliable colour and red-fruit flavour.

The other way, saignée or maceration, leaves crushed black grapes on their skins for a short time until the juice turns pink. It gives deeper colour and more structure, and is rarer.

Most of our rosés, Moët, Taittinger, Paul Bara, Chartogne-Taillet and Veuve Fourny, use the blending method. Rosé Champagne has a little more body than white, so it suits salmon, duck and the Bananas Foster.

changes.before: Ageing on the lees
changes.after: Aging on the lees

changes.before:
Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation. Leaving a wine in contact with them, instead of drawing it off, slowly changes it: the cells break down and release compounds that add a creamy texture, roundness and flavours of bread, brioche and toast.

In Champagne and every traditional method wine the lees age inside the bottle, which is where the toasty notes and fine, creamy bubbles come from; the longer, the finer. In Muscadet the wine rests on its lees in tank through the winter, sur lie, and the best for two years or more, gaining body and a savoury depth.

So when a guest asks why a Champagne tastes of brioche, the answer is the lees, not oak or added flavour.

changes.before:
Most Champagne is fermented in steel tanks, which keeps the fruit pure. A few houses ferment some or all of their base wines in oak barrels instead, the old way, which adds roundness, a gentle oxidative richness and a toasty, nutty depth.

Sous Bois means under wood: Billecart-Salmon's Sous Bois has every base wine fermented in oak. Bollinger ferments part of its wine in old barrels, which is one reason its Special Cuvée is so rich and structured; Krug ferments in small old casks too.

Our Billecart-Salmon Sous Bois magnum, labelled for Brennan's 80th anniversary, and the Bollinger Special Cuvée show the style. Say: richer and nuttier, a Champagne for food.

changes.before:
Great white Burgundy is usually fermented and aged in small oak barrels, about 228 litres, called pièces. Oak lets in a little air, which rounds the wine, and new barrels add toast, vanilla and spice; most growers use only a share of new oak so the fruit stays in front.

Many also stir the lees in the barrel, bâtonnage, for a creamier texture. The richness of Meursault, the hazelnut of Puligny and the toast of the best California Chardonnay come from this cellar work as much as from the grape.

On our list, Jadot's Meursault, Lafon, Leflaive, Carillon, Pillot, Kongsgaard and Au Bon Climat use barrels; Dauvissat ages part in old oak; the Fichet Château London has only a touch of old oak. Ask a guest whether they like oaky or crisp before you choose.

changes.before:
Most fine reds spend months or years in oak barrels. The wood lets in a trickle of air, which softens tannin and deepens colour, and new barrels add their own flavour.

French oak, tight-grained, gives subtle cedar, spice and toast; it is the choice of Bordeaux, Burgundy and most Napa Cabernet. American oak, more open-grained, gives sweeter vanilla, coconut and dill, and is traditional in Rioja and for Zinfandel. Large old casks, as at Pegau, add little flavour and simply let the wine breathe.

La Rioja Alta's 904 ages about four years in American oak from its own cooperage; Ridge's Lytton Springs uses American oak; Duckhorn, Talbot and the Bordeaux use French. Vanilla and coconut say American; cedar says French.

changes.before:
All red grape juice is clear; the colour lives in the skins. To make rosé the winemaker controls how long the juice touches the skins.

For pale Provence rosé, the black grapes are pressed straight away, gently, so the juice picks up only the faintest blush: direct pressing. A short maceration of a few hours before pressing gives a deeper pink and more body. Picking early and keeping the juice cold keeps the freshness.

Minuty and Whispering Angel are pale, direct pressed rosés: peach, strawberry and citrus. The Tempier Bandol rosé and Pascal Cotat's Chavignol rosé have more colour and structure. Colour is a hint, not a promise of sweetness: all four are dry.

Goldkapsel, gold capsule, is a German grower's signal, not a legal category. A grower bottles a richer, more concentrated selection of the same Prädikat, usually from riper or botrytised berries, and dresses it with a gold foil capsule. A long gold capsule, lange Goldkapsel, marks an even finer selection.

So a Goldkapsel Auslese is richer and sweeter than the same grower's plain Auslese, and usually made in small amounts, often in half-bottles.

Our gold capsule wines are Dönnhoff's two Auslesen from the Brücke and the Hermannshöhle, Prüm's Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese in magnum and Dr. Hermann's Würzgarten Kranklei Spätlese. Point to the capsule when you present the bottle.

An off-dry wine has a little sugar left in it, enough to taste as a soft roundness but not as dessert. In a high-acid grape like Riesling the acidity balances the sugar, so the wine tastes juicy rather than sweet.

German growers use feinherb, or halbtrocken, for wines just off dry. The Berres Old Vines by the glass carries about twenty grams of sugar a litre at only 11.5 per cent alcohol; Stein's Weihwasser and Palmberg-Terrassen are feinherb.

Off-dry wine is a server's secret weapon with Creole spice, smoke, sweet glazes and the maple on the duck: the touch of sugar cools heat that would make a dry wine taste bitter and hot.

Botrytis cinerea is a mould that, in the right weather, becomes noble rot. It needs misty, humid autumn mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The mould pierces the grape skins and the sun dries the berries, which shrivel, losing water while the sugar and acidity concentrate.

The grapes look ruined but make the most luscious sweet wines in the world, tasting of honey, apricot, candied orange, saffron and marmalade. Because the rot spreads unevenly, pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking only the affected berries.

Sauternes and Barsac, Burgenland, the Loire and the highest Prädikat levels in Germany depend on it. On our list: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens, Gilette, Kracher, Keller and the Grgich Violetta.

Late harvest wine is made from grapes left on the vine well after the normal picking date, so they lose water, shrivel a little and concentrate their sugar. Some are also touched by noble rot.

The result is sweet wine with the grape's own flavours deepened: honeyed apricot, baked fruit and spice. In Alsace it is called Vendanges Tardives and is allowed only for the four noble grapes in years ripe enough; in California and Italy it is simply late harvest.

Ours are Trimbach's Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives, Ridge's Essence Zinfandel, the Grgich Hills Violetta and Banfi's Florus Moscadello. Each is made only in years the weather allows.

Appassimento is the Italian art of drying freshly picked grapes before pressing. In Valpolicella the best bunches are laid on bamboo racks or in shallow crates, or hung, in airy lofts for three or four months over the winter.

The grapes lose much of their water and turn half to raisins, concentrating sugar, colour and flavour. Fermented fully dry they make Amarone; stopped while still sweet they make Recioto.

Giuseppe Quintarelli dried his grapes this way on racks and in crates, and our Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997 is the result: dark cherry, fig, raisin and chocolate, sweet and velvety, with fresh acidity.

A vin doux naturel, naturally sweet wine, is made by stopping fermentation partway by adding neutral grape spirit, a process called mutage. The yeast dies, so the grape's own unfermented sugar stays in the wine, and the alcohol rises to about 15 to 18 per cent. Port is made the same way.

In Roussillon, Banyuls and Rivesaltes are then aged either fresh and fruity, or oxidatively for years in old casks or glass demijohns left out in the sun, turning amber and tasting of fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

The La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva on the dinner tasting is aged the oxidative way; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 has spent decades in old casks. Banyuls with chocolate is the classic match.

changes.before:
Port is made in the Douro by stopping the fermentation of red grapes with grape spirit when about half the sugar has turned to alcohol. The young wine is sweet, strong at about 20 per cent and deeply coloured.

Because fermentation is cut short, the colour and tannin must be pulled from the skins fast, so the grapes are trodden by foot in shallow stone tanks called lagares or worked in modern machines that copy it.

Then the style is set by ageing. Ruby styles, including Late Bottled Vintage and Vintage Port, age briefly in large casks and keep their dark fruit; tawny styles age for years in small casks, turning amber and nutty. Our list carries every kind.

Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, is Port from a single year, like Vintage Port, but left in wood much longer, four to six years, before bottling. The longer cask time softens it and makes it ready to drink sooner.

Most LBV is filtered and ready on release; traditional unfiltered LBV keeps ageing and may throw a little sediment. It gives much of Vintage Port's dark fruit at a gentler price.

Ours are unusual: Feist's 2006 and Sandeman's 1999 have had long bottle age on top of their years in wood, so they are mature and mellow: dark cherry, plum, fig, cocoa and spice. Check for sediment and decant if any.

Tawny Port ages for years in small, old casks, where slow contact with air turns its colour from ruby to amber and its fruit to walnut, caramel, dried orange peel and coffee. Most tawnies are blends, sold as 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old.

A Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, colheita in Portuguese, aged at least seven years in cask and often far longer, with the harvest year and the bottling date on the label. Because it has aged with air in cask, it needs no decanting and keeps for weeks once opened.

Niepoort, a family house of Dutch origin, is famous for its Colheitas. Ours is the 1997 in a half-bottle. Serve it slightly cool with pecan desserts and the Bread Pudding.

A field blend is a vineyard planted with several grape varieties mixed together, row by row or vine by vine, then picked and fermented together. The blend is made in the vineyard, not in the cellar.

It was the old way in Europe and in early California, where Italian and other immigrant growers planted Zinfandel with Petite Sirah, Carignane, Grenache, Mataro and others for balance: one for colour, one for acidity, one for fruit.

Ridge's Lytton Springs, planted from 1901 and holding more than twenty varieties, is a textbook example, and Ridge's Three Valleys draws on old field grapes too. When a guest asks what is in it, the label lists the share of each grape.

Organic farming grows vines without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilisers, using cover crops, compost and copper or sulphur sprays. Biodynamic farming goes further, following the ideas of Rudolf Steiner from the 1920s: it treats the vineyard as a living whole, uses herbal and mineral preparations and plans work by a lunar calendar.

Growers say it brings livelier soils and wines that show their place more clearly. Some are certified; others farm this way without a label.

Leflaive in Burgundy became a leader of biodynamic farming from 1997; Huet, Climens and d'Angerville farm biodynamically; Gouges, Saint Damien and Pépière organically; Châteaumar organically without certification. Describe the farming; never make a health claim for the wine.

Rioja labels promise how long a wine has aged before release. Crianza has at least two years, one of them in oak. Reserva has at least three, one in oak. Gran Reserva, made only in good years, has at least five, with at least two in oak and the rest in bottle.

Traditional houses go well beyond the minimums. The long ageing softens the tannin and turns the fruit savoury: dried cherry, strawberry, tobacco, leather, vanilla and sweet spice.

La Rioja Alta ages its Gran Reserva 904 about four years in American oak barrels from its own cooperage, then years in bottle before release. It is the bottle for a guest who loves mellow, old-style red with lamb or duck.

changes.before:
A bottle of Champagne holds about six atmospheres of pressure, roughly three times a car tyre, so it is opened with care, and quietly.

Chill it to 43 to 46°F. Present the label to the host. Loosen the cage but keep a thumb or a napkin over the cork from then on. Hold the bottle at about 45 degrees, pointed away from guests, grip the cork and turn the bottle, not the cork, easing it out so it leaves with a soft sigh rather than a pop.

Pour a little into each glass to let the foam settle, then top up to about two thirds, guests first and the host last. Return the bottle to the ice bucket, half ice and half water.

The Coravin system lets us pour a glass of a fine still wine without pulling the cork. A thin, hollow needle passes through the cork; the bottle is pressurised with argon, an inert gas, which pushes the wine out through the needle. When the needle is withdrawn, the natural cork closes up again and the argon protects the wine left inside.

So a bottle such as the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé can be poured by the glass over weeks without spoiling, and a guest can taste a great white Burgundy without buying the bottle.

At the table, say: poured by Coravin, so the bottle is never opened. Present the label. Who handles the device and the house's limits are questions for the bar.

A magnum holds 1.5 litres, two standard bottles; a double magnum, called a Jeroboam in Champagne, holds 3 litres, four bottles. Larger bottles still have Biblical names, such as Rehoboam and Methuselah.

Wine ages more slowly and gracefully in large bottles, because there is less air for each drop of wine, which is why collectors prize them. And nothing makes a table's toast like a magnum.

Our large formats include the Billecart-Salmon 80th anniversary magnum, the Bollinger and Piper-Heidsieck magnums, the Taittinger double magnum and Prüm's Auslese in magnum. Carry it with both hands, open it like any Champagne, pour in small first pours, and keep it in a deep bucket.

changes.before:
A mature wine has spent years, sometimes decades, ageing in bottle. Its fruit turns from fresh to dried, its tannin softens, and new notes appear: leather, forest floor and mushroom in reds; honey, nuts and petrol in Riesling; caramel and coffee in Port.

Mature bottles need gentle handling. Carry them as they lay, without shaking; stand older reds and Ports upright ahead of time if you can; open slowly, as old corks crumble, and keep a two-pronged cork puller or a decanter ready. Taste for soundness with the sommelier before pouring for the table.

Our list is rich in age: Pichon Lalande 2004, Beaucastel 2007, Gilette 1989, Riveyrac 1975, Taylor 1977 and more. Tell guests the age is the point: they are drinking time.

A corked wine has been tainted by a compound called TCA, usually from the cork. It smells of wet cardboard, a damp cellar or a musty basement, and the fruit seems flat and muted. It affects a small share of bottles sealed with natural cork, and it is never anyone's fault at the table.

When the host tastes and frowns, smell the cork and the glass, or ask the sommelier to. If the wine is faulty, apologise, take the bottle away and bring another, without debate.

Other faults are rarer: a bottle that is oxidised, flat and brown, or cooked by heat. A wine the guest simply dislikes is a different matter, for the sommelier or manager to handle.

Brennan's wine cellar is one of the few in the world to hold Wine Spectator's Grand Award, the magazine's highest honour, given for depth, breadth, mature vintages and harmony with the menu. The house's own notes say it first won the award in 1983.

Then came Hurricane Katrina in 2005. A month without power cooked the cellar, and about 35,000 bottles were lost. After the restaurant reopened, the team rebuilt the collection, and the house notes say it won the Grand Award back in 2021; reports of the 2025 awards name it again, with about 3,000 to 3,600 selections, deepest in Burgundy, Champagne, Bordeaux and California.

Every bottle you present comes from that rebuilt cellar. Confirm the award years from the listing at lineup before quoting them.

Piper-Heidsieck was founded in Reims in 1785 by Florens-Louis Heidsieck, a cloth merchant from Westphalia who set out to make a cuvée worthy of a queen and presented his wine to Marie Antoinette. After his death his nephew's partner, Henri-Guillaume Piper, joined the business, and the two names were joined.

Today Piper-Heidsieck makes our house Champagne, an Extra Brut of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay bottled under the Brennan's name, poured by the glass and by the bottle, and its Cuvée Brut in magnum on Birthday Bubbles.

Say labelled for us, not made for us; Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel, and which cuvée is in the bottle, and its dosage, is for the sommelier to confirm.

By the 1970s much Beaujolais was industrial, sugared and fermented with cultured yeast. A small band of growers in the village of Villié-Morgon set out to change that, inspired by the oenologist Jules Chauvet: Marcel Lapierre, Jean Foillard, Jean-Paul Thévenet and Guy Breton, nicknamed the Gang of Four by their American importer.

They went back to old vines, late picking, whole bunches, native yeasts and little or no added sulphur, and their silky, vivid Morgon wines became a root of the natural wine movement. Lapierre's children run his estate now.

We pour the Lapierre Morgon and Foillard's Côte du Py. Coudert's walled Clos de la Roilette in Fleurie is a family estate in the same spirit of fine, honest Gamay.

Château de Beaucastel has been run by the Perrin family since 1909. Lulu's Provençal cooking, generous and seasonal, inspired Alice Waters of Chez Panisse and a generation of American chefs; she died in 2020 aged 102. Their family still owns the domaine.

The Wehlener Sonnenuhr, the Wehlen sundial, is one of the Mosel's most famous vineyards, a steep slope of grey Devonian slate facing south across the river. In 1842 Jodocus Prüm, a vineyard owner, built a large sundial into the rock so the workers on the slope could tell the time, and the vineyard took its name.

The Prüm family has been in Wehlen for centuries; the Joh. Jos. Prüm estate dates from 1911, when the family's holdings were divided. Its Rieslings are delicate, lightly sweet and famously long-lived, sometimes with a little spritz when young.

We pour the Wehlener Sonnenuhr Kabinett 2020 and the gold capsule Auslese 2015 in magnum.

Inniskillin was founded on the Niagara Peninsula of Ontario in 1975, with the first new winery licence granted there since Prohibition, as the house tells it. Its founders, an Austrian-born winemaker and a Canadian nurseryman, set out to make Canadian icewine on European lines.

The word Parmesan means different things on either side of the Atlantic. In the European Union, a 2008 ruling of the European Court of Justice held that only Parmigiano Reggiano, the protected cheese of Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and parts of Mantua and Bologna, may be sold as parmesan. Its rules are strict: cows fed on fresh fodder and hay, no silage, no preservatives, dairies that make nothing else, and inspection at twelve months.

In the United States, Parmesan is a generic name. The federal standard of identity describes a granular cheese with a hard, brittle rind that grates readily, at most 32 per cent moisture and cured at least ten months; it says nothing about where the cheese is made.

So when an American menu prints Parmesan, as Brennan's does in the creamed spinach of the Eggs Sardou, it promises a hard grating cheese, not a particular one. The kitchen may use Parmigiano Reggiano, the Grana Padano it buys for the Caesar and the Shells & Cheese, which has its own card, or a domestic Parmesan. A server should know the difference and find out which.

Creekstone Farms began in 1995, when John and Carol Stewart set up a purebred Black Angus farm in Campbellsburg, Kentucky. Stewart was a cattle geneticist at heart: he developed his own Angus line, sold bulls, genetics and semen to ranchers, and at one point owned the highest-marbling bull in the breed.

In 2003 the company moved into processing, buying a processing plant in Arkansas City, Kansas, where it began processing its own Premium Black Angus cattle in May 2003. Its cattle-receiving facility was the first built from the ground up to the low-stress handling standards of Dr. Temple Grandin. After BSE was found in the US herd in December 2003, Creekstone asked in 2004 to test every animal it slaughtered, and when the USDA refused, it took the question to court.

Stewart announced his retirement in October 2006. Sun Capital Partners had owned the business since 2005, and in 2017 it sold Creekstone to the Japanese trading house Marubeni Corporation, which owns it today. The company still buys its cattle on verifiable Black Angus genetics rather than hide colour, and its Natural Black Angus line carries the Certified Humane label.

At Brennan's the name is printed on three plates: both hanger steaks and the tenderloin of the Roasted Chateaubriand.

The Rohan is D'Artagnan's own duck. D'Artagnan was founded in 1985 by Ariane Daguin and George Faison, who met working at a charcuterie shop in New York City. A farmer had the first domestically raised foie gras in the United States and needed someone to sell it, so the two started a company to do it, selling whole raw lobes to New York chefs. Daguin was born in Auch, in Gascony, the eldest child of the Michelin-starred chef André Daguin, and the company is named for the Gascon musketeer. It is based in Union, New Jersey.

D'Artagnan's blog introduced the Rohan in January 2012. It is a proprietary cross of several breeds, including the heritage Mallard and the Pekin, bred to approximate a style of duck found in Normandy and named for the family of dukes and princes of Rohan in Brittany. The birds are raised for D'Artagnan on a farm in New York's Catskills, cage-free and never given antibiotics, hormones or steroids, to 11 weeks, five weeks longer than the average factory duck. Daguin says the extra time deepens the flavour and improves the meat-to-bone ratio.

The result is rosy, tender, mild meat with a rich, buttery depth. Brennan's prints Rohan on the duck breast of the dinner tasting and on the confit leg of the Duck Confit Waffle.
